decisions.quote:
This research replicates an earlier study (O’Connor, Beach, Sanchez, Bocian, & Flynn, 2015)

and extends it by shifting instructional responsibility from researchers to special education

teachers, who implemented reading instruction that included multisyllabic word decoding,

academic vocabulary, and three comprehension strategies (generating main ideas, comparing and

contrasting people, and events, and identifying cause and effect relations) with their intact 8th grade

history classes, using history text as the reading material. Participants included 73 8th grade

students with disabilities (77% with Learning Disabilities; 72% male, 45% English Language

Learners) and four teachers. Compared to students with disabilities in typical special education

history classes, students in the treatment outperformed controls on researcher-developed measures

of word- and text-level reading comprehension, as well as in the history content that students in

both conditions studied.
decisions.reason: This study is a completed empirical replication that collects new data from 73 eighth-grade students with disabilities across four middle schools to re-test the BRIDGES intervention of O’Connor, Beach, Sanchez, Bocian, & Flynn (2015; doi: 10.1177/0014402914563706), shifting instructional delivery from researchers (Year 2 of the original study) to special education U.S. history teachers (pp. 2, 8-9). The paper explicitly states that the original study found strong student gains in decoding, vocabulary, comprehension strategies, and U.S. history content knowledge (pp. 8-9, 24, 28), and reports that students in the BRIDGES treatment significantly outperformed business-as-usual controls across all three instructional cycles on decoding accuracy, receptive and expressive vocabulary, all three comprehension strategies (main idea, compare and contrast, and cause and effect on both taught and transfer passages), and end-of-cycle U.S. history content tests (pp. 2, 22-25, 28-31). Both the shipped and blind codings correctly record the replication outcome as 'successful'.
